title: Magneto-oscillations, nonlinearity, and nonreciprocity of Coulomb drag in quantum circuits
authors: Alex Levchenko, Mingyang Zheng, Dominique Laroche
abstract: We consider the problem of Coulomb drag in interactively coupled quantum circuits built of adiabatic constrictions: quantum point contacts and short quantum-wire channels. The interplay of spatial confinement and magnetic field leads to a rich oscillatory response of the drag current as a function of gate voltage and magnetic field: drag peaks track the depopulation of magnetoelectric subbands, are asymptotically periodic in inverse field, and their visibility is controlled by the competition of temperature with the field-sharpened tunneling width of the constriction. We derive a closed expression for the linear drag conductance whose interaction kernel simplifies dramatically in the experimentally relevant limit of a long thermal length compared with the range of the interwire coupling, investigate the drag in the nonlinear regime, where the drag current measures the transconductance of the drive channel at any field, and discuss physically motivated models of dissipation-induced nonreciprocity of the drag signal. Extensions accounting for Zeeman splitting, interaction renormalization of the barrier transmission, backscattering at high field, and the frequency structure of the circuit coupling delineate how each mechanism imprints itself on the temperature dependence and lineshapes of the drag oscillations.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive theory for Coulomb drag in coupled quantum wires under a magnetic field. It predicts characteristic magneto-oscillations whose contrast depends on temperature relative to the field-sharpened tunneling width. Furthermore, it rigorously analyzes nonlinear and nonreciprocal transport effects, providing diagnostic tools for characterizing device physics beyond simple linear response.
main_problem: The study investigates magneto-oscillations, nonlinearity, and nonreciprocity effects in Coulomb drag within interactively coupled quantum circuits.
main_result: The theory derives closed forms for the linear drag conductance and shows that nonlinear/nonreciprocal responses are governed by transconductance measurements or geometric asymmetries.
method: The analysis employs Keldysh scattering-state constructions, Landauer formalism extensions, and detailed derivations in both linear (thermal) and nonlinear (shot noise) transport regimes.
model_or_system: The system consists of two interactively coupled adiabatic constrictions (quantum point contacts or short quantum wires) embedded in a magnetic field. The coupling is modeled purely by the Coulomb interaction.
key_observables: Magneto-oscillations in drag current, linear drag conductance ($g_D$), particle-hole asymmetry factor ($A_i(\omega)$), and nonreciprocal components of the drag signal.
important_parameters: Magnetic field ($B$) leading to cyclotron frequency ($\omega_c$), temperature ($T$), gate voltage ($V_g$), and the ratio of thermal length to coupling range ($L_T/d$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes a minimal system of two coupled constrictions, uses approximations for the interaction kernel in different limits (e.g., long thermal length), and analyzes specific transport regimes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate magnetoconductance staircase structures dependent on confinement ratios, show periodicity in $1/B$, map parameter space showing drag ridges tracking subband steps, and compare theoretical predictions for temperature dependence ($T^2$ vs. linear-in-$T$).
paper_structure: The paper builds from the basic Hamiltonian and single-particle solutions to derive the linear drag conductance using Keldysh techniques. It then extends this analysis to the nonlinear regime (shot noise) and discusses distinct sources of nonreciprocity, concluding with open problems regarding zero-field asymmetry and low-temperature upturns.
why_interesting: The detailed theoretical framework for analyzing mesoscopic transport phenomena like Coulomb drag in magnetic fields is highly relevant to understanding quantum coherence and interaction effects in nanoscale electronic devices, bridging concepts from condensed matter theory and quantum optics.
